summary: Describes using the ACAP protocol to configure wireless devices over the air, covering activation and provisioning of phones. It is an informational paper and replaced RFC 2604.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2636 describes how a mobile carrier could set up and update a phone over the radio. Instead of using dedicated telephone equipment, the carrier runs a small configuration server on its own data network and the phone fetches its settings from it, using the ACAP protocol. The memo also works through how activation works in practice and what each side has to be able to do.

questions: how does acap provision a phone
subtitle: How a carrier could provision and update CDMA phones over the air using ACAP, a small Internet configuration protocol.

tldr.problem: Handset activation and parameter updates were expensive, because they needed dedicated EIA/TIA/IS-683A equipment and a trip to the point of sale, while carriers were moving handset sales into the retail channel.
tldr.mechanism: The memo puts the provisioning data in an ACAP server on the carrier's IP network, reachable over the IS-707 data service that carriers are already deploying, with a small ACAP client in the handset, a shared secret derived from the A-key, and a data tree that lets roaming lists be inherited from regional and device-class datasets.
tldr.outcome: The data formats stay identical to IS-683A so handset code can be reused, and the approach can run alongside a WAP-based mechanism, with the ACAP server as the single source of provisioning data.

facts.label: Authentication Key (A-key)
facts.value: A secret 64-bit pattern stored in the mobile station

facts.label: Shared Secret Data (SSD)
facts.value: A 128-bit pattern known to the network and stored in the mobile station

facts.label: Electronic Serial Number (ESN)
facts.value: A 32-bit number assigned by the handset manufacturer

facts.label: Mobile Identification Number (MIN)
facts.value: The 10-digit directory number of a mobile station

facts.label: Activation dial string
facts.value: *228 XX, the N-digit password and SEND

facts.label: Baseline ACAP authentication
facts.value: Keyed-MD5 with a server challenge, published as RFC 2195

today: RFC 2636 is an Informational memo published in July 1999. It was later updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Why Over-the-Air Provisioning
sections.content:
The memo starts from a business problem. Carriers face creating more efficient distribution channels, increasing customer satisfaction, and improving margin and profitability, while industry trends push the sale of handsets further into the retail channel. The cost and effort of provisioning handsets, activating users and updating handset parameters can be greatly reduced by using over-the-air activation mechanisms, and a comprehensive and extensible means for over-the-air provisioning and handset parameter updating is required.

One approach is to purchase EIA/TIA/IS-683A equipment, the Over-the-air Service Provisioning of Mobile Stations in Spread Spectrum Systems. The cost has led carriers to seek alternative solutions. The approach in the memo is to use the IS-707 data services equipment that most carriers are in the process of deploying, delivering provisioning and parameter upgrading over it. The protocol used is ACAP, the Application Configuration Access Protocol, an Internet protocol that provides remote storage and access of configuration and preference information.

The memo argues that a well thought-out approach using Internet-based open standard mechanisms provides an extensible platform for further carrier service offerings, better interoperability among back-end services, and vendor independence.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a mobile phone has meant a trip to a shop, with special equipment at the carrier's end. The memo proposes doing it over the air instead, using the data network the carrier already has and a small open Internet protocol to carry the settings.

sections.title: What OTASP and OTAPA Do
sections.content:
OTASP, Over-the-air Service Provisioning, allows a potential wireless service subscriber to activate new wireless services, and allows an existing wireless subscriber to make service changes without the intervention of a third party. It includes a way to establish a user profile, over-the-air programming of a Number Assignment Module, IMSI and roaming lists including data option parameters, and optionally service provider or manufacturer specific parameters such as a lock code or call timer. It also includes an Authentication Key generation procedure and A-key storage.

OTAPA, Over-the-air Parameter Administration, allows a wireless service provider to update a NAM, IMSI and roaming list information in the mobile station remotely, again without the intervention of a third party. The memo says this capability increases flexibility and reduces costs for carriers involved with mass changes that affect every handset, such as area-code splits. OTAPA covers updating a user's NAM, data option parameters, service provider or manufacturer specific parameters such as server addresses, lock code or call timer, and roaming lists.
sections.plainLanguage: OTASP is the first-time setup of a phone: the carrier writes the account details and the security key into the handset over the radio. OTAPA is the same thing later on, when the carrier pushes new settings to many handsets at once, such as after an area code is split.

sections.title: How Provisioning Happens
sections.content:
A new subscriber gives the intended service provider enough information to prove creditworthiness and establish a record in the provider's billing system, and the ESN of the mobile station has to reach the provider as well. The memo describes three ways this happens. In the voice scenario a customer care representative collects credit information during a call made from another phone or initiated using the IS-683A OTASP dialling scheme of the form *228xx. Once the user is authorized, the representative creates a record in the CDMA network HLR, so the network can be used, and a limited-time N-digit password is created and tied to the ESN, with the choice of N a trade-off between security and user inconvenience. All required provisioning information, including the password, is loaded into the provisioning server, and the user is told to hang up and call a special number of the form *228 XX, the N-digit password and SEND. That makes the mobile station start a provisioning session: the mobile station and the provisioning server authenticate, the required provisioning information is downloaded into the mobile station, and the user receives a notification, which can be an audible tone or a text message on the display.

In the forms scenario an interactive user interface is presented through a browser on the mobile station and the subscriber fills in the requested information, though entering non-numeric data presents user interface challenges on many mobile devices. A back-end server validates the information and, if possible, authorizes the customer, generates the limited-time password and creates the HLR and provisioning server records; otherwise a voice call is made to a customer care representative. In the desktop scenario the subscriber uses a desktop or in-store kiosk web browser to contact the carrier and enter the usual personal information, and the carrier's server validates it, creates the records, and tells the subscriber to dial the special number on the handset.

Users already authorized for the CDMA network can also start provisioning activity, after being directed to do so by a customer care representative, for instance when the carrier wants to upgrade CDMA parameters in the handset or when troubleshooting is needed; the mobile station downloads the new information in the same way. OTAPA activity is initiated at the customer care centre, usually by queuing a notification to the mobile station, via one-way SMS or a special caller-ID, after the provisioning server holds the updated configuration data, and it will not occur until the mobile station has acquired CDMA service on the carrier's network and the notification has reached it. Alternatively a recheck interval can be included in the provisioning data, so that a mobile station checks in periodically to see whether anything has changed. OTAPA activity can be terminated at any time due to user call activity.
sections.plainLanguage: The first setup usually starts with a person or a web form collecting the subscriber's details, after which the carrier creates the account and gives the user a short code. The user dials that code on the handset, the handset and the carrier's server authenticate each other, and the settings are written into the phone.

sections.title: What the Network and the Handset Must Support
sections.content:
IS-683A OTASP operations occur between a mobile station and an over-the-air service provisioning function using IS-95A traffic channel data burst messages. Doing OTASP and OTAPA over data services requires a CDMA carrier network with IS-707 data services capability, either Packet Data Service or Quick-Net-Connect. The mobile station must support the IS-707 data service capability, the Packet or QNC RLP protocol, PPP to the IS-707 IWF, IP to provide the network layer for routing to the provisioning server, a transport layer for end-to-end communication such as TCP, authentication and optionally encryption, application software to handle the provisioning protocol and memory access, and DNS query capabilities sufficient to obtain the address of the provisioning server, whose address could alternatively be provided during PPP negotiation. The mobile must also be able to make a data call, and optionally a voice call, without a MIN.

OTASP over data services uses a provisioning server holding the parameter information for the mobile stations. The authorizing agent at the customer care centre has to be able to add user and mobile station information to both the CDMA network HLR and the provisioning server during the initial authorizing process, and the provisioning server must be able to service a mobile as soon as its record is created. OTAPA by contrast is performed by a mobile-terminated call that downloads parameters without user interaction: the network has to direct the mobile station to make a special-purpose data call, for example after a mobile-terminated one-way SMS message whose content the mobile station parses to know when to originate the OTAPA call, and the user is not informed of the call activity.

The provisioning server replaces the IS-683A OTAF and resides on an IP network inside the carrier's own network. It must perform all the service provisioning and parameter administration functions the OTAF provides, and have an interface to the carrier's Mobile Terminal Authorizing System, serving to synchronize the provisioning server with the information in the MTAS and to make provisioning information immediately available for downloading. A standard ACAP server provides an excellent means of meeting these requirements. The memo also considers two alternatives and explains why it prefers ACAP: porting IS-683A to TCP would need a custom-built server with no data manipulation of its own, and browser-based forms would need a provisioning-capable browser in every phone plus a meta-protocol with no time for open review.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone needs a data connection that reaches the carrier's IP network, and the carrier needs a server that holds each handset's settings and stays in step with its own customer database. The memo's point is that both can be built from standard Internet pieces.

sections.title: The Provisioning Server and the ACAP Data Model
sections.content:
The architecture has three parts: a provisioning server in the carrier's intranet that supports ACAP, an administrative client in the customer care domain that updates that server using ACAP, and a small ACAP client in the handset that is provisioned and configured through it. ACAP was designed for exactly this kind of job, with protocol simplicity, support for thin clients and ease of operation over limited bandwidth among its primary goals, and a high degree of extensibility in authentication mechanisms, specialized attribute handling and data management. The administrative client can use the same simple protocol to load and modify the server as the handsets use for provisioning, which simplifies the client and makes it independent of the server.

ACAP organizes data by datasets, whose structure is defined by the dataset class; generally the server has no knowledge of dataset classes, so a dataset can be expanded without modifying the server. Datasets contain entries, and entries contain attributes and values; any entry can also be a dataset, so the data is hierarchical. ACAP also supports inheritance: data items physically in an inherited dataset and not in the inheriting dataset logically exist in the inheriting dataset, and this is recursive, so a large group of mobile stations can inherit items from a single common entity. Preferred roaming lists, for example, can be stored in datasets based on geographic areas and inherited automatically by a mobile station in that area, and the mobile client need not be aware of it.

For provisioning, the data sits in the OTAP dataset class, with the prefix Provision. for items downloaded to the mobile and Client. for items the client stores on the server. Each provisioning item is stored in its own entry, the entry name is the item name, and the OTAP.VALUE attribute holds the value, which permits change notification on a per-item basis. Provisioning records are identified by the ESN and the NAM in use, and the standard location is /OTAP/USER/<esn>/<nam>/, which allows multiple NAMs per ESN. The entries hold data in IS-683A parameter block types: the CDMA NAM as 13 or more octets of binary data, the mobile directory number as a string of 10 or more ASCII digits, and IMSI_T left-justified in 7 octets. The data can be organised to use items identical to IS-683A, so that handset engines can be reused.

The mobile client then runs a short exchange. After authenticating it issues a SEARCH for the OTAP.Requested-Data attribute to learn which items the server wants it to report, and stores one attribute per requested item, with the value the mobile has or the special value [N/A] if the item does not exist or is unknown on the mobile. It then issues a SEARCH for provisioning entries whose name begins with provision. and whose modification time is greater than the one it supplied, which in an initial session retrieves everything, writes the returned values into its non-volatile memory, and stores the returned modification time on the server as an acknowledgement that the data was received. The client then logs out and closes the TCP connection, ending the data call.
sections.plainLanguage: All the settings for every handset live in one server, arranged as a tree. A handset holds a very small program that logs in, fetches the settings that have changed since last time, and writes them into its own memory.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
OTASP requires an authentication procedure to validate the mobile station to the provisioning server, while OTAPA requires a mechanism where the mobile validates the server. The mobile client authenticates with the ACAP server before performing any activities, using the mobile's ESN and a shared secret: a provisioned mobile derives the shared secret from the A-key, and an unprovisioned mobile uses the limited-time password as the secret. The baseline ACAP mechanism uses the shared secret plus a random challenge from the server as input to a one-way cryptographic hash function, specifically keyed-MD5, which is the CRAM-MD5 mechanism published as RFC 2195, and it is analogous to the existing IS-683A mechanism that uses a random challenge and the CAVE algorithm. An A-key is generated using a Diffie-Hellman exchange, as in IS-683A, and the provisioning server can either generate A-keys itself that way or receive them from the carrier network. ACAP includes an authentication framework, SASL, which allows any standard or custom authentication and encryption mechanism to be used, so that stronger mechanisms can be added later without disrupting the deployed clients and servers.

Because data OTASP and OTAPA operate over IP within the carrier's network, end-to-end encryption between the mobile station and the provisioning server should be considered as a future enhancement. Such encryption protects against attacks from within a carrier's network and safeguards the provisioning data, for example the roaming lists. The memo's own security section notes that security is discussed in many parts of the document, and that the need and methods to guard against unauthorized updating of handsets, usurpation of newly created accounts, compromise of handset security values, and disclosure of carrier proprietary data and handset parameters are covered.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone has to prove it is entitled to the settings before it is given them, using a secret key and a challenge from the server. The memo also says that encryption across the whole path should be added later, because it protects the roaming lists and other carrier data from anyone inside the carrier's own network.

messages.label: SEARCH OTAP.Requested-Data
messages.note: Ask which items the server wants the handset to report back.

messages.label: REQUESTED-DATA VALUES
messages.note: For example phone-make, phone-model, SW-Rev and Free-NVRAM.

messages.label: STORE CLIENT ATTRIBUTES
messages.note: One attribute per requested item, with the mobile value or the special value [N/A].

messages.label: SEARCH PROVISION.*
messages.note: Ask for provisioning items changed since the last check-in.

messages.label: VALUES AND MODTIME
messages.note: The provisioning values, plus the modification time of the newest entry.

messages.label: STORE MODTIME
messages.note: Acknowledge that the values were written to the handset's memory.

messages.label: LOGOUT
messages.note: Then the client closes the TCP connection and the data call ends.
